questions.explanation: After the final file is assembled, documentation must not be deleted or discarded before the end of the retention period. If it is necessary to add to or modify the file, the auditor must document the specific reasons, when the changes were made and reviewed, and by whom. Silent replacement would undermine the integrity of the audit record.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the fundamental principles in the ICAEW Code of Ethics?

options.A: Integrity
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Professional behaviour
options.D: Independence

questions.explanation: The five fundamental principles are integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour. Independence is closely linked to objectivity and is required of auditors and other assurance providers under the independence requirements, but it is not itself one of the five fundamental principles.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: Which fundamental principle requires a professional accountant to be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships?

options.A: Integrity
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Professional behaviour
options.D: Professional competence and due care

questions.explanation: Integrity means being straightforward and honest, so an accountant should not knowingly be associated with misleading information. Objectivity concerns not allowing bias, conflicts of interest or undue influence to override judgement. Professional behaviour involves complying with laws and avoiding conduct that discredits the profession.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: An audit firm prepares a client's financial statements and then audits them. Which threat to objectivity does this create?

options.A: Advocacy
options.B: Intimidation
options.C: Familiarity
options.D: Self-review

questions.explanation: A self-review threat arises when the firm evaluates its own previous work, as the audit team may fail to identify, or be reluctant to report, errors in statements their firm prepared. Advocacy involves promoting the client's position, intimidation involves pressure on the auditor, and familiarity arises from close relationships.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: A senior partner has acted as audit engagement partner for the same client for many years and has developed close friendships with its directors. Which threat does this create?

options.A: Self-interest
options.B: Familiarity
options.C: Self-review
options.D: Advocacy

questions.explanation: Long association with a client can create a familiarity threat because the partner may become too sympathetic to the directors and less sceptical. A common safeguard is rotating senior personnel off the engagement. Self-interest involves financial or other personal interests, and self-review involves checking the firm's own work.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: The finance director of an audit client tells the audit partner that the company will change auditors unless the partner agrees to a favourable accounting treatment. Which threat does this create?

options.A: Familiarity
options.B: Intimidation
options.C: Self-review
options.D: Advocacy

questions.explanation: An intimidation threat arises when the auditor is deterred from acting objectively by actual or perceived pressure, such as a threat of dismissal. The partner should not give in to the pressure and should consider discussing the matter with those charged with governance and others within the firm.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: An audit firm promotes the shares of an audit client to potential investors. Which threat does this create?

options.A: Intimidation
options.B: Familiarity
options.C: Self-review
options.D: Advocacy

questions.explanation: An advocacy threat arises when the firm promotes a client's position to the point that its objectivity may be compromised. Promoting the client's shares aligns the firm with the client's interests, which is incompatible with the independent role of the auditor.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: An audit manager has inherited shares in a company that the firm audits. What is the appropriate action?

options.A: The manager can stay on the audit provided the shareholding is disclosed in the auditor's report
options.B: The manager should dispose of the shares as soon as practicable or be removed from the audit team
options.C: No action is needed because the shares were inherited rather than purchased
options.D: The manager should buy more shares so that the holding is clearly disclosed to the board

questions.explanation: A direct financial interest in an audit client creates a self-interest threat so significant that no safeguard other than disposal or removal from the team is adequate. The way the shares were acquired does not change the threat, although it allows a short period to dispose of them. Disclosure in the auditor's report is not an acceptable safeguard.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: Fees from one audit client form a large and growing proportion of an audit firm's total fee income. Which threat arises and which safeguard is most appropriate?

options.A: A self-interest threat; disclose the position to those charged with governance and arrange an independent review of the audit work
options.B: A self-review threat; ask the client to prepare its own financial statements
options.C: A familiarity threat; rotate the junior staff on the audit
options.D: An advocacy threat; decline to represent the client in disputes with HM Revenue & Customs

questions.explanation: Fee dependence creates a self-interest threat, because the firm may be reluctant to upset a client whose fees it cannot afford to lose. Appropriate safeguards include disclosure to those charged with governance and an engagement quality review by someone outside the team, or reducing the work for the client. The other threats and safeguards do not address economic dependence.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: An audit client offers the audit team free tickets to a major sporting event as thanks for their work. What should the audit team do?

options.A: Decline the tickets unless their value is trivial and inconsequential
options.B: Accept the tickets because the audit has already been completed
options.C: Accept the tickets provided the audit partner attends as well
options.D: Accept the tickets and disclose them in the auditor's report

questions.explanation: Gifts and hospitality from an audit client create self-interest and familiarity threats. They should be accepted only if a reasonable and informed third party would consider them trivial and inconsequential. Valuable tickets to a major event are unlikely to meet this test, and disclosure in the report is not an acceptable safeguard.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: Which of the following fee arrangements for a statutory audit would be unacceptable?

options.A: A fee based on the time spent by staff at agreed hourly rates
options.B: A fee calculated as a percentage of the client's reported profit before tax
options.C: A fixed fee agreed in advance, reflecting the expected work
options.D: A fee that increases because the client's business has grown and the audit involves more work

questions.explanation: A contingent fee, where the fee depends on the outcome of the work or a result such as reported profit, creates a self-interest threat so significant that it is not permitted for an audit. Time-based fees, fixed fees and fees reflecting the work required are all acceptable, provided the fee is sufficient to allow a proper audit.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: An accountant's advertising claims that the firm 'guarantees to cut your tax bill by half'. Which fundamental principle is most likely to be breached?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Professional competence and due care
options.D: Professional behaviour

questions.explanation: Professional behaviour requires accountants to avoid conduct that discredits the profession, including making exaggerated claims about the services they can offer. A guarantee of a particular tax saving cannot be honestly given. Confidentiality and objectivity are not directly affected by the advertising claim.

questions.topic: Professional ethics: principles, threats and safeguards
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the conceptual framework approach to ethics in the ICAEW Code?

options.A: Follow a complete list of prohibited activities, as anything not listed is permitted
options.B: Identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles, evaluate their significance, and eliminate them or reduce them to an acceptable level, declining or ending the work if this is not possible
options.C: Accept all threats, provided they are disclosed to the client in the engagement letter
options.D: Refer every ethical issue to the client's audit committee for a decision

questions.explanation: The Code uses a principles-based conceptual framework rather than a complete set of rules. Accountants identify threats, evaluate them using the reasonable and informed third party test, and address them by eliminating the circumstances, applying safeguards or declining the engagement. Disclosure alone, or passing decisions to the client, does not meet these requirements.

questions.question_text: In which of the following situations is an accountant REQUIRED to disclose confidential client information?

options.A: When the accountant knows or suspects that the client is engaged in money laundering and must make a report
options.B: When a journalist asks for details of the client's financial results
options.C: When a potential investor in the client asks for information
options.D: When another client asks about the creditworthiness of the client

questions.explanation: Confidential information must not be disclosed without proper authority unless there is a legal or professional right or duty to disclose. UK law requires accountants in the regulated sector to report knowledge or suspicion of money laundering. Requests from journalists, investors or other clients do not create a duty to disclose and could breach confidentiality.

questions.question_text: During an audit, a senior learns that the client is about to make a takeover bid for a listed company. The senior buys shares in the target company. Which fundamental principle is primarily breached?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Professional competence and due care
options.C: Objectivity
options.D: Professional behaviour only, as the information was not disclosed to anyone

questions.explanation: Confidentiality prohibits using information obtained through professional work for personal advantage, as well as disclosing it. Using the information to buy shares breaches this principle and may also amount to insider dealing. It is not only a matter of professional behaviour, because the information was used even though it was not disclosed.

questions.question_text: A criminal deposits cash from drug dealing into several bank accounts in small amounts. Which stage of money laundering does this illustrate?

options.A: Layering
options.B: Placement
options.C: Integration
options.D: Concealment

questions.explanation: Placement is the initial stage, where criminal proceeds, often cash, are introduced into the financial system. Layering involves complex transactions to hide the source of the funds, and integration is when the funds re-enter the legitimate economy appearing clean.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the 'layering' stage of money laundering?

options.A: Introducing cash proceeds of crime into the banking system
options.B: Using the funds to buy legitimate assets so they appear clean
options.C: Carrying out complex transactions to obscure the link between the funds and their criminal source
options.D: Reporting the funds to the authorities

questions.explanation: Layering involves moving funds through a series of transactions, such as transfers between accounts or jurisdictions, to make the audit trail difficult to follow. Introducing cash is placement, and using funds to buy legitimate assets is integration.

questions.question_text: An accountant reports a suspicion of money laundering by a client to the firm's money laundering reporting officer. Afterwards the accountant tells the client that a report has been made. Which offence may the accountant have committed?

options.A: Failure to report
options.B: Placement
options.C: Tipping off
options.D: Breach of the duty of care

questions.explanation: Tipping off is the offence of disclosing that a report has been made, or that an investigation is under way, where this is likely to prejudice an investigation. The accountant did make the required report, so there has been no failure to report. Placement is a stage of money laundering rather than an offence by the accountant.

questions.question_text: How should an employee of an accountancy firm report a suspicion of money laundering by a client?

options.A: Directly to the client's board of directors
options.B: In the auditor's report to the shareholders
options.C: To the firm's money laundering reporting officer, who decides whether to make a report to the National Crime Agency
options.D: To the firm's marketing partner, who will decide whether to continue acting for the client

questions.explanation: Regulated firms must appoint a nominated officer, usually called the money laundering reporting officer. Staff make internal reports to this officer, who considers them and decides whether to submit a suspicious activity report to the National Crime Agency. Informing the client could amount to tipping off.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the offence of failing to report money laundering by a person in the UK regulated sector is correct?

options.A: The offence is committed only if the person had actual proof of money laundering
options.B: The offence does not apply to accountants, only to banks
options.C: The offence can be committed where there were reasonable grounds to know or suspect money laundering, even if the person did not actually suspect it
options.D: The offence applies only where the amount involved exceeds the audit materiality level

questions.explanation: For the regulated sector the test is objective as well as subjective: a person who should reasonably have known or suspected money laundering may commit an offence by not reporting. Proof is not required, the regulated sector includes accountants and auditors, and there is no materiality threshold for reporting suspicions.

questions.question_text: In the UK, which type of body is responsible for registering and monitoring firms eligible to carry out statutory audits, such as ICAEW?

options.A: A recognised qualifying body only
options.B: A recognised supervisory body
options.C: The Registrar of Companies
options.D: HM Revenue & Customs

questions.explanation: Statutory auditors must be members of a recognised supervisory body, which registers eligible firms and monitors their audit work through inspections, under oversight by the competent authority. A recognised qualifying body awards the audit qualification. The Registrar of Companies and HM Revenue & Customs do not regulate auditors.

questions.question_text: An accountancy firm is asked to advise two clients who are competing to buy the same business. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Advise both without telling either, as long as the work is done well
options.B: Always advise the client who pays the higher fee
options.C: Share each client's bid strategy with the other so that both are treated equally
options.D: Advise both only if the conflict is disclosed, both clients consent, and safeguards such as separate teams and information barriers are applied

questions.explanation: Acting for competing clients creates a conflict of interest that threatens objectivity and confidentiality. The firm may continue only if the threats can be reduced to an acceptable level, normally by disclosure, obtaining consent and using separate teams with information barriers. Sharing information would breach confidentiality, and choosing by fee level is not an ethical basis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following situations is most likely to give an accountant grounds to suspect money laundering under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002?

options.A: A client makes a genuine arithmetical error in its VAT return and corrects it promptly
options.B: A client deliberately fails to declare income to HM Revenue & Customs and keeps the tax saved
options.C: A client chooses a tax-efficient pension contribution permitted by law
options.D: A client makes a loss on a legitimate investment

questions.explanation: Under the Act, criminal property includes any benefit from criminal conduct, including money saved through deliberate tax evasion. Retaining the tax saved therefore involves criminal property, and an accountant aware of it would need to consider reporting. Honest mistakes that are corrected, legal tax planning and investment losses are not criminal conduct.

questions.question_text: What is the auditor's responsibility for events occurring between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report?

options.A: No responsibility, because the audit covers only the financial year
options.B: To guarantee that no significant events have occurred
options.C: To prepare the disclosures of any events identified
options.D: To perform procedures designed to identify events that may require adjustment of, or disclosure in, the financial statements

questions.explanation: The auditor must perform procedures, such as reviewing board minutes and management accounts and making inquiries, to identify subsequent events that need adjustment or disclosure. The directors remain responsible for preparing the disclosures. No guarantee can be given that all events have been found.

questions.question_text: Which of the following events occurring after the reporting date would normally be an adjusting event?

options.A: A major customer that owed the company money at the year end goes into liquidation
options.B: A fire destroys a warehouse two months after the year end
options.C: The company announces a plan to close a division after the year end
options.D: The company issues new shares after the year end

questions.explanation: An adjusting event provides evidence of conditions that existed at the reporting date. The customer's liquidation shortly after the year end usually shows that the receivable was already impaired at the year end. The fire, the closure announcement and the share issue arise from conditions after the year end, so they are non-adjusting, although they may need disclosure if material.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most likely to cast doubt on a company's ability to continue as a going concern?

options.A: A small increase in staff turnover
options.B: A change of the company's external auditor
options.C: The payment of a dividend in line with previous years
options.D: The loss of its largest customer and the bank's refusal to renew its overdraft facility

questions.explanation: Losing a key customer reduces future cash inflows, and losing bank finance removes a source of funding, so together they may mean the company cannot pay its debts as they fall due. Small changes in staff turnover, a change of auditor or a normal dividend are not, on their own, indicators of going concern problems.

questions.question_text: In an unmodified auditor's report on the financial statements of a UK company, what does the auditor's opinion state?

options.A: Whether the company's internal controls are effective
options.B: Whether the company will be profitable next year
options.C: Whether every transaction has been recorded correctly
options.D: Whether the financial statements give a true and fair view and have been properly prepared in accordance with the applicable framework and the Companies Act 2006

questions.explanation: The opinion on UK company financial statements covers whether they give a true and fair view and have been properly prepared in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework and the Companies Act 2006. The audit opinion does not certify internal control, predict future profits, or confirm that every transaction is correct.

questions.question_text: An auditor concludes that inventory is materially overstated but the effect is not pervasive. The directors refuse to adjust it. What type of opinion should be given?

options.A: An adverse opinion
options.B: A disclaimer of opinion
options.C: A qualified opinion
options.D: An unmodified opinion with an emphasis of matter paragraph

questions.explanation: Where misstatements are material but not pervasive, the auditor gives a qualified 'except for' opinion. An adverse opinion is used where misstatements are both material and pervasive, and a disclaimer is used when the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects could be material and pervasive. An emphasis of matter paragraph does not modify the opinion.

questions.question_text: Because of a fire that destroyed most of the client's accounting records, the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence over most balances, and the possible effects are both material and pervasive. What type of opinion should be given?

options.A: An adverse opinion
options.B: A disclaimer of opinion
options.C: A qualified opinion
options.D: An unmodified opinion with an emphasis of matter paragraph

questions.explanation: When the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive, the auditor does not express an opinion. A qualified opinion is used if the possible effects are material but not pervasive. An adverse opinion relates to misstatements that have been identified, not to a lack of evidence.

questions.question_text: An auditor concludes that the financial statements contain misstatements that are both material and pervasive, and management refuses to correct them. What type of opinion is required?

options.A: A disclaimer of opinion
options.B: A qualified opinion
options.C: An adverse opinion
options.D: An unmodified opinion with an other matter paragraph

questions.explanation: If the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence and concludes that misstatements are both material and pervasive, the opinion is adverse: the financial statements do not give a true and fair view. A disclaimer relates to a lack of evidence, and a qualified opinion is used where the effect is material but not pervasive.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about an emphasis of matter paragraph is correct?

options.A: It is used to qualify the opinion where there is a material misstatement
options.B: It draws users' attention to a matter properly presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is fundamental to their understanding, and does not modify the opinion
options.C: It replaces the opinion paragraph where evidence is insufficient
options.D: It is used to disclose matters that the directors have refused to disclose

questions.explanation: An emphasis of matter paragraph highlights a matter that is appropriately presented or disclosed, such as a major uncertainty, which is fundamental to users' understanding. It is not a substitute for a modified opinion: if a matter is misstated or not disclosed properly, the opinion itself must be modified.

questions.question_text: When should the written representations obtained from management be dated?

options.A: On the last day of the financial year
options.B: At the start of the audit fieldwork
options.C: At least three months after the date of the auditor's report
options.D: As near as practicable to, but not after, the date of the auditor's report

questions.explanation: Written representations should cover all periods referred to in the auditor's report and be dated as near as practicable to, but not after, the date of that report. This ensures they cover events up to the date the opinion is given. Representations dated earlier would not cover the full period, and later ones would be too late to support the opinion.
